text.description: A short herd path from the same junction as Street Mountain, usually climbed with it. Path: Nye ski trail and herd path via Indian Pass Brook. Starts at Adirondak Loj / High Peaks Information Center.
Unmarked path leaves the Bradley Pond trail about 4.3 miles in; often combined with Santanoni. Path: Bradley Pond Trail and Panther Brook herd path. Starts at Upper Works, Newcomb.
Heavily used marked trail leaving the Marcy route past Marcy Dam; a good first High Peak. Path: Van Hoevenberg Trail and Phelps Trail. Starts at Adirondak Loj / High Peaks Information Center.
Most climbers go over Giant and along the ridge; a longer direct route starts at the East Trail on Route 9. Path: Roaring Brook Trail over Giant, then the ridge trail.
Steps and ladders on the Ore Bed Trail; the garden lot is small and fills early on weekends. Path: Johns Brook Valley and Ore Bed Trail. Starts at The Garden, Keene Valley.
Steep eroded herd path after the marked trail to Bradley Pond; Santanoni Brook can be hard to cross when wet. Path: Bradley Pond Trail and Santanoni Express herd path. Starts at Upper Works, Newcomb.
Out-and-back on a marked trail with a steep rock slab; the reserve needs a parking reservation in season. Path: Weld Trail. Starts at St. Huberts parking (Adirondack Mountain Reserve).
Marked trail for about 5 miles, then an unmarked eroded path; the road can be closed in winter. Path: Blueberry Trail to Seward herd path. Starts at Corey's Road parking area.

Cairned herd path leaves the truck trail just past the Ward Brook lean-to; steep and slippery on top. Path: Blueberry Trail, Ward Brook Truck Trail and Seymour herd path. Starts at Corey's Road parking area.
Unmarked herd path with a steep dip and bare-rock climb; also called Carson Peak. Path: Dix Range crest herd path from Elk Lake. Starts at Elk Lake trailhead.

Unmarked and brushy; the unbridged brook crossing can be dangerous at high water. Done with Nye in one trip. Path: Nye ski trail and herd path via Indian Pass Brook. Starts at Adirondak Loj / High Peaks Information Center.

name: Herd path from the Van Hoevenberg Trail

text.description: Unmarked herd path leaving the main trail past Marcy Dam; frequently paired with Phelps. Path: Herd path off the Van Hoevenberg Trail. Starts at Adirondak Loj / High Peaks Information Center.

Steep and often icy on the upper part; a longer alternative starts at The Garden via Johns Brook. Path: West River Trail, Wedge Brook Trail and State Range Trail cutoff. Starts at St. Huberts parking (Adirondack Mountain Reserve).

text.approach: Start at the Pioneer Gulch trailhead and follow the Pioneer Gulch Trail until it meets the Diamond Peak Trail. Leave the trail there and head straight uphill, trending toward climber's left, until you reach the southwest ridge. In winter, with the Summit Lake road shut, this is the easiest line to reach. In mid-May snow can still cover the forest road from about 4,900 ft, adding road miles on snowshoes, while the first mile of trail is often already bare.
text.overview: Easiest access when snow closes the Summit Lake road, and a handy way in for skiers after the bowls beneath the top. The trailhead at Pioneer Gulch gives a round trip of 7.5 miles and gains somewhat over 4000 feet. Hike until the trail joins the one named for Diamond Peak, then go directly uphill bearing climbers left to the southwest ridge. Stay on it until it merges with the south ridge, and continue to the top.

A bold 1974 line: hard aid on poor limestone in a remote spot, with one night in a hammock and another on a ledge. Rock is poor and dangerous, hauling is much work, and the whole face totals about 1200 ft. A 1990s free attempt reached 300 ft. Another attempt took a different variation from the route on the left, freeing a different way to begin after drilling two bolts, the rock being rotten and wet. text.approach: Mowich Lake has had no road access since the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge closed in April 2025, with no detour; reaching the lake now means a long walk in on the Wonderland Trail from another part of the park. From Mowich Lake, take the Wonderland Trail 4 miles to Spray Park. Climbers trail ascends lower Ptarmigan Ridge. At 8,300 ft, descend 1,000 ft to North Mowich Glacier.

text.overview: A northwest-facing ice/snow face route above Mowich Lake, with an easier original line (Grade III) and a harder, more direct variation (Grade IV) both topping out on the Liberty Cap glacier.
text.description: Central Mowich Face offers two route variations on the northwest face of Mount Rainier. Route follows steep snow and ice sections on a north-facing glacier. Two main variations exist: Grade III (direct, snow-dominant) and Grade IV (ice-steep variation).
text.descent: From Liberty Cap or the main summit, descend via Emmons-Winthrop to Camp Schurman, or via Disappointment Cleaver to Camp Muir, depending on party preference and conditions.

text.overview: A Grade IV ice route on the northwest side climbing directly up the North Mowich Glacier headwall to Liberty Cap, with a short rock band crux partway up.
text.description: North Mowich Headwall (Edmunds Headwall) is a steep Grade IV ice and mixed route on the north side of Mount Rainier. Features sustained steep slopes and narrow hourglass rock/ice section.
text.descent: From Liberty Cap, cross to the main summit area or descend directly via Emmons-Winthrop to Camp Schurman.

text.overview: A more remote alternative to the standard route, gained from the glacier below the peak's northeast face and climbing mixed snow and rock — including a large, ~45-degree snow gully — via mostly class 3 with occasional class 4 rock to the summit.
Seven pitches, climbing the buttress that stands out on the left of Tungsten Lake.

text.approach: Same south-face approach as Beckey-Tate: park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20, follow the Kangaroo Temple/Wallaby Peak path along Early Winters Creek, cross the creek, and ascend the approach gully (left fork at the high Y-junction) to the base of the Beckey-Tate start, then traverse right across overlaps to the route's own start ledge.

text.overview: A five-pitch line on the south face sharing the Beckey-Tate approach before traversing right to two clean corner pitches, including a burly 5.11c bulge, then finishing up easier cracks to the top of the wall.
text.descent: From the top of the route, join the standard descent: scramble to the notch just north of the true summit, then follow the loose scree-and-snow gully back down toward the Hairpin pullout, roughly two hours from the top.

text.approach: Park at the Hairpin pullout on SR-20 (roughly Milepost 163, about 1 mile east of Washington Pass). Follow the Kangaroo Temple/Wallaby Peak climbers' path south along Early Winters Creek for roughly 2 miles, then leave the trail to cross the creek and ascend the prominent gully system to the base of the south face, taking the left fork at the high Y-junction. Expect 2.5 to 5 hours of approach time; water is unreliable late season.

text.overview: A longer, harder companion line to Beckey-Tate on the south face's southeast buttress, following crack systems up variable-quality granite to a sustained 5.11a finger-crack crux; one of the more popular technical routes on the peak despite the wall's overall obscurity.
text.descent: As with the neighboring Beckey-Tate line, descend by scrambling to the notch just north of the true summit and following the loose scree-and-snow gully back down toward the Hairpin pullout, roughly two hours from the top.

text.descent: The standard descent is the Beckey-Tate walk-down (scramble to the notch, then the loose gully back to the Hairpin pullout). text.overview: A serious ground-up aid-and-free line up blank, overhanging roof systems nicknamed 'the Kangaroofs' low on the south face, established over three days in August 2012, with natural-gear free climbing above the bolted aid pitches.
text.descent: The first-ascent team bivied on the summit after topping out at 2 a.m. and descended the following morning via the Beckey-Tate line — scrambling to the notch just north of the summit, then following the loose scree-and-snow gully back toward the Hairpin pullout (roughly two hours from the summit).

text.approach: Start at the Dingford Creek Trailhead and hike the Dingford Creek Trail about 3.2 miles to the junction with the Hester Lake Trail. Leave the Myrtle Lake branch there and take the Hester Lake side, then leave the path and work cross-country toward the mountain's southwest ridge. Expect brush, steep forest and route-finding with no maintained tread.
